title: Arapahoe Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Arapahoe wells have a 322-foot median depth, with finished costs estimated at $17,300-$29,700.
h1: Arapahoe, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Arapahoe means looking closely at the well record, not just assuming a plains property will have dependable water. Permits within five miles show a median well depth of 322 feet and a median reported yield of 22.5 gallons per minute, but the records are uneven: 177 wells are listed, 60 are recorded as constructed, and only 38 report a pump yield.

Most permits identify either an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer or the Ogallala. That mix makes neighboring records useful, but not conclusive for a new lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact site, intended use, access, casing and grout requirements, pump setting, and water-quality concerns before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Arapahoe wells usually reach the deeper plains zones
sections.html:
The local depth pattern is fairly consistent compared with many rural areas. The median reported depth is 322 feet, and the middle half runs from 298 to 362 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 385 feet, while the deepest record reaches 410 feet. No recorded wells are under 100 feet or above 600 feet; 75% fall in the 300-to-600-foot range and 25% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

For a drilling bid, that means a proposal near the local median should not be based on a shallow-hole assumption. The final depth can change with the target formation, water-bearing fractures, casing and grout design, and the result of drilling. Records near Cheyenne Wells, Sheridan Lake, or Kit Carson may provide useful regional context, but Arapahoe-area wells are the better comparison.

sections.heading: Reported yield is generally strong, but the record is limited
sections.html:
Among the 38 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 22.5 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute, and 84% report more than 15 gallons per minute. The low-yield tail still matters: 3% are under 1 gallon per minute, another 3% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 11% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Those figures describe reported well performance, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage capacity, and intended household or irrigation demand. A strong test rate can still require proper pump sizing and pressure storage. Irrigation accounts for 47% of the recorded use mix, while domestic or household use accounts for 20%.

sections.heading: Arapahoe water-level records are too sparse for a trend
sections.html:
Only 2 wells report a static water level, so the local dataset cannot show a reliable water-table trend by decade. Those reported measurements have a median depth to water of 234 feet, with the middle half from 218 to 249 feet. Treat that as a limited snapshot rather than proof that groundwater is rising, falling, or stable across Arapahoe.

The aquifer labels also vary. Permits identify 119 wells in an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 52 in the Ogallala, and 1 in the Dakota. Fractured formations can be unpredictable over short distances, even when nearby wells look similar. Before buying, compare static water levels and completion details from adjoining parcels, then have a qualified driller assess the proposed location.

sections.heading: Permit history points to a long-running local drilling market
sections.html:
Arapahoe has a long permit history, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s. The largest recorded decades are the 1980s with 25 permits and the 1970s with 22. There are 2 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit year in the records is 2023. The use mix is led by irrigation at 47%, followed by stock at 32% and domestic or household use at 20%.

The most active drillers in these records are Kemp's Well Service, listed with 29 wells; Schaal Drilling Co., with 13; and Hasz Energy & Development Co., with 6. These names show who appears in the permit history, not who is available or best for a current project. Confirm licensing, insurance, schedule, references, and the scope of the written proposal before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Arapahoe well needs a realistic budget
sections.html:
For ground described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the local drilling model uses a rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 322-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $11,300 to $17,700. That is the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $17,300 to $29,700 at the median depth. A quote can move outside that range if the hole runs deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more electrical or trench work. Request an itemized bid that separates drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, pressure storage, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: PFAS and low-yield questions deserve attention before closing
sections.html:
Environmental review is important around Arapahoe. Mapping shows 55 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That mapping does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it is a reason to obtain current water-quality testing and investigate nearby land uses, drainage, and well history. Historic mine features are recorded at 0 in the mapped area.

Also check for dry-hole history, low-yield wells, abandoned wells, and septic setbacks before finalizing a building plan. A well that produces water may still be poorly suited to a larger home, livestock, or irrigation without adequate storage. Confirm the permit allows the planned use. If a basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses. Review septic soil conditions and well-to-septic separation with the county and qualified contractors.

sections.heading: What to verify on an Arapahoe lot before you buy
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then collect completion reports for nearby wells rather than relying on the area median alone. Compare depth, aquifer name, static water level, tested yield, pump setting, and permitted use. The local records contain 177 permits, but only 102 report total depth and only 38 report pump yield, so missing information is common.

For a vacant lot, make the water plan part of due diligence. Get a driller's site review, a written cost range, and a plan for access, electrical service, trenching, septic placement, and storage. For an existing home, test the water and inspect the pump, pressure tank, casing, and wellhead. Ask how the well performed during dry periods and whether the recorded permit matches current use. These checks are more useful than treating a nearby 322-foot well as a guarantee.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Arapahoe, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Arapahoe is 322 feet. The middle half of reported wells runs from 298 to 362 feet, with the 90th percentile at 385 feet and the deepest record at 410 feet. Most are in the 300-to-600-foot range, while 25% are between 100 and 300 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Arapahoe?
faq.a: The drilling model for Arapahoe uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 322 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $11,300 to $17,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $17,300 to $29,700, before site-specific changes or unusual conditions.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Arapahoe?
faq.a: Among 38 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 22.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute. Records show 84% producing above 15 gallons per minute. Still, 3% are under 1 gallon per minute, so a buyer should review the actual neighboring well reports.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Arapahoe, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit record alone. Mapping shows 55 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not prove a specific well is affected. Have the well tested for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest if the property or water conditions change.

faq.q: Who drills wells near Arapahoe, Colorado?
faq.a: The most active drillers in the permit records are Kemp's Well Service, listed with 29 wells; Schaal Drilling Co., with 13; and Hasz Energy & Development Co., with 6. These are historical permit-record counts, not recommendations or proof of current availability. Verify licensing, insurance, references, scope, and pricing before selecting a contractor.
